name: Comprehension and intent
description: A reader can build a correct mental model of the code from its naming, structure, documented contracts, and stated assumptions, without reconstructing hidden intent from implementation detail.
details:
Comprehension is not a single property. Apparent purpose, precise domain naming, aligned levels of abstraction, documented public contracts, comments that justify rather than narrate, locally followable control flow, cohesive function shape, justified complexity, freedom from tribal knowledge, and explicit assumptions all belong to one lens because they are answered by the same act: reading the code the way the next maintainer will read it. A change can be functionally correct and still fail this lens badly, and the failure is invisible to tests.

Strong signs include names drawn from the vocabulary the domain, tests, and documentation already use; units that operate at one conceptual level instead of mixing policy with formatting and low-level detail; interfaces that state their guarantees, constraints, error cases, and side effects; comments that explain a tradeoff or non-obvious constraint; control flow a reader can hold in their head without chasing distant context; functions whose parameters reflect their true responsibility; and assumptions or structural decisions recorded where the reader will need them. Weak signs include vague or overloaded names, abstraction levels smeared together, easy-to-misuse public surfaces left undocumented, comments that restate the code, deeply nested or sprawling control flow, functions doing several jobs at once, indirection the problem does not require, and correctness that depends on norms only long-time contributors know.

This lens matters because comprehension is the precondition for every other kind of review. A reader who cannot form a correct model of the code cannot judge its correctness, cannot change it safely, and cannot tell an intentional decision from an accident. Judge whether the change makes intent easier to see and rely on, or whether it raises the interpretation cost paid by everyone who reads the code later.
symptoms:
SYM-001 | Intent is obvious | A reader can understand what this unit is for without reverse engineering the whole surrounding system.
SYM-002 | Names are domain-specific and precise | Names use the language of the domain and distinguish meaning clearly enough that readers do not have to infer intent from surrounding context.
SYM-005 | Levels of abstraction are aligned | A unit of code operates at one conceptual level at a time instead of mixing policy, orchestration, formatting, and low-level detail.
SYM-006 | Public contracts are documented | Public or easy-to-misuse interfaces explain their guarantees, constraints, error cases, side effects, and expected usage.
SYM-007 | Comments explain why | Comments justify intent, tradeoffs, or non-obvious constraints rather than narrating what the code already says.
SYM-008 | Code is easy to follow locally | Control flow and structure are linear and bounded enough that a reviewer can understand a unit without chasing large amounts of external context.
SYM-009 | Function shape is cohesive and tractable | A function has one clear job, stays small enough to understand as a whole, and takes a set of inputs that reflects its true responsibility.
SYM-020 | Complexity and control flow are justified | The solution has no more abstraction, branching, indirection, or special-case handling than the problem actually requires.
SYM-048 | Reviewers do not need tribal memory | Correctness does not depend heavily on undocumented norms that only long-time contributors know.
SYM-063 | Assumptions, intent, and structural decisions are explicit | The code and its surrounding artifacts make assumptions, change intent, and important architectural decisions visible enough that reviewers and future maintainers do not have to reconstruct them from guesswork.

name: Domain modeling and data expressiveness
description: Types, signatures, and data structures express domain concepts and the invariants that govern them, instead of flattening meaning into primitives, flags, and generic containers that invite misuse.
details:
How a system represents its concepts decides how many mistakes are possible in it. Explicit types for domain concepts, meaningful return values, structurally protected invariants, avoidance of boolean blindness and primitive obsession, data shapes that match real access patterns, and clear ownership of data all belong to one lens because they are read from the same place: declarations, signatures, and the shape of the data that moves between them. Representation is where correctness is either designed in or left to discipline.

Strong signs include domain concepts that have their own types rather than being carried as bare strings, numbers, or maps; return values that communicate outcome and meaning without ambiguous booleans, magic values, or overloaded null; states whose invalid combinations cannot be constructed or persisted; named concepts or richer types where flag arguments would otherwise hide intent; data structures whose shape reflects how they are actually used and what must remain true of them; and one obvious authority for each piece of data. Weak signs include stringly-typed domain values, repeated primitives standing in for concepts that deserve first-class representation, boolean parameters that force readers to the definition, generic containers passed through many layers, invariants maintained only by convention or by remembering to call something, and data whose authoritative owner is unclear or contested.

This lens matters because weak representation converts design problems into runtime problems. When the model is precise, whole classes of defect become unrepresentable and the compiler or schema does the reviewing. When it is vague, every call site becomes a place where the invariant can be broken, and the cost is paid in defects and defensive checks forever. Judge whether the change makes the domain harder to represent incorrectly, or whether it pushes meaning out of the model and into the heads of callers.
symptoms:
SYM-003 | Concepts have explicit types | Important domain concepts are represented explicitly rather than being flattened into vague primitives, strings, flags, and maps.
SYM-011 | Return values are meaningful | Outputs communicate useful meaning rather than ambiguous booleans, magic values, or overloaded null semantics.
SYM-014 | Invariants are protected | The code structure makes invalid states difficult or impossible to represent or persist.
SYM-023 | Boolean blindness is avoided | Flags and ambiguous booleans are not used where richer types or named concepts would express intent better.
SYM-024 | Primitive obsession is avoided | Repeated low-level primitives do not stand in for richer domain concepts that deserve first-class representation.
SYM-025 | Data shape matches behavior | Data structures reflect access patterns and invariants instead of being generic containers that invite misuse.
SYM-065 | Data ownership is clear | It is obvious which component or service is authoritative for a given piece of data or business rule.

name: State effects and failure behavior
description: Runtime behavior is legible and safe: what mutates and who owns it, what must happen in what order, what enters from outside, and what happens on every failure path.
details:
This lens follows execution rather than structure. Visible side effects, absence of hidden state, clear ownership of mutation, input stopped at the boundary, intentional and consistent error semantics, explicit temporal coupling, controlled nondeterminism, complete resource handling, correctness under concurrency and retries, resilience to partial failure, and intentional recovery paths all belong together because answering any of them means tracing the same paths through the change: what happens, in what order, with what state, and what happens when it goes wrong.

Strong signs include functions whose effects are apparent from their surface rather than discovered by reading their bodies; state with an obvious owner, lifecycle, and set of allowed transitions; external input validated, normalized, and rejected at the boundary before it can spread; failures surfaced deliberately and consistently so callers can act on them; required ordering encoded or enforced instead of socially remembered; time, randomness, and external variability injected rather than reached for; resources released on both success and failure paths; operations safe to repeat or interleave, with atomicity where the domain needs it; degraded dependencies handled proportionally; and restart, retry, replay, or rollback stories that exist where they matter. Weak signs include ambient mutable state and invisible caches, mutation with no clear owner, validation deferred until the data is deep inside the system, swallowed or reclassified exceptions, arbitrary local error styles, order dependencies that only comments or habit protect, direct clock and random access in logic, leaks on the error path, retries that duplicate effects, and a single dependency failure that collapses the whole request.

This lens matters because these defects are the ones that survive review and appear in production. They are usually invisible on the happy path, disproportionately expensive to diagnose after the fact, and often only reproducible under load, failure, or unlucky ordering. Judge whether the change makes runtime behavior easier to predict and safer when something goes wrong, or whether it adds behavior that only holds while nothing unusual happens.
symptoms:
SYM-010 | Side effects are visible | A reader can tell whether a function mutates state, performs I/O, logs, throws, retries, or causes other external effects.
SYM-012 | Hidden state is avoided | A unit does not rely on ambient mutable state, invisible caches, implicit globals, or surprising external mutation.
SYM-013 | Mutation has a clear owner | When state changes, the owner, lifecycle, and allowed transitions are obvious.
SYM-015 | Untrusted or invalid input is stopped at the boundary | External input is validated, normalized, sanitized, and rejected early enough that invalid or unsafe state does not spread through the system.
SYM-016 | Error semantics are intentional and consistent | Failures are surfaced in deliberate, diagnosable, and system-consistent ways, without silent semantic drift, swallowed exceptions, or arbitrary local error styles.
SYM-017 | Temporal coupling is explicit | If operations must happen in a particular order, that requirement is encoded or enforced rather than socially remembered.
SYM-018 | Nondeterminism is controlled | Time, randomness, concurrency, and network variability are explicit and testable rather than leaking unpredictably into logic.
SYM-019 | Resource handling is complete | Files, sockets, locks, transactions, and other resources are acquired and released correctly on both success and failure paths.
SYM-031 | Correctness under concurrency, transactions, and retries is explicit | The code makes ordering, atomicity, and safe re-entry understandable so concurrency, transaction handling, and repeated execution do not create hidden correctness risks.
SYM-066 | The system is resilient to partial failure | Dependency failure, timeout, bad input, and degraded subsystems do not cause disproportionate collapse.
SYM-067 | Recovery paths are intentional | Restart, retry, replay, rollback, and repair stories exist where the domain requires them.

name: Structure boundaries and dependencies
description: The arrangement of modules reflects real responsibilities: related things live together, variation and shared rules have one owner, and dependencies point the right way through narrow contracts.
details:
Structure is judged by mapping the change onto the system around it. Cohesive placement, intentional or absent duplication, localized points of variation, explicit and well-shaped module interactions, single ownership of shared rules, boundaries and layers that follow real responsibilities, a design not dictated by its framework, and preserved architectural integrity all belong to one lens because they are read from the same view: which modules exist, what each is responsible for, and what depends on what and why.

Strong signs include logic, data, and rules that belong together living together; repeated logic either eliminated or justified deliberately; variation confined to narrow explicit seams instead of conditionals spread through many files; collaborators visible in constructors, parameters, or declared boundaries; dependencies pointing inward toward stable policy rather than outward toward storage and transport detail; each core rule defined in exactly one authoritative place; layers that separate policy from mechanism because the responsibilities really differ; framework choices confined to the edges; and domain concepts that stay inside their context unless deliberately translated. Weak signs include related rules scattered across distant layers, copy-paste variants drifting apart, flag checks smeared through the codebase, hidden collaborators reached through locators or broad context objects, high-level policy depending on low-level detail, the same rule restated in several modules and their tests, layering that mirrors technical convenience rather than responsibility, designs that exist only because the framework works that way, and utility sprawl that becomes the real center of gravity.

This lens matters because structure determines the cost of every future change. When boundaries match responsibilities, edits stay local and readers can predict where behavior lives. When they do not, work spreads unpredictably, the same rule diverges in several places, and the system becomes a mesh of hidden assumptions that no one can safely refactor. Judge whether the change leaves the structure a more faithful description of the system's responsibilities than it found it.
symptoms:
SYM-004 | Related things live together | Logic, data, and rules that belong together are not scattered across distant files or layers.
SYM-021 | Duplication is intentional or absent | Repeated logic is either eliminated or clearly justified, rather than copied accidentally across the codebase.
SYM-022 | Variation is localized | When behavior varies, the points of variation are narrow and explicit rather than smeared through conditionals everywhere.
SYM-026 | Dependencies and module interactions are explicit and well-shaped | Collaborators, dependency direction, coupling, cohesion, and interface shape work together so modules depend on the right things, for the right reasons, through narrow and comprehensible contracts.
SYM-027 | Shared rules have a single owner | Core rules are defined in one authoritative place rather than being re-stated in multiple modules and tests.
SYM-028 | Boundaries and layers reflect real responsibilities | Module boundaries, layering, boundary crossings, and separation of policy from mechanism are arranged so the structure of the system matches its real responsibilities instead of incidental technical detail.
SYM-029 | Framework does not own the design | The architecture is not merely a mirror of the chosen framework's defaults or constraints.
SYM-064 | Architectural integrity is preserved across domains and interfaces | The architecture keeps a clear organizing principle, respects domain boundaries, preserves intent across APIs and integrations, resists drift, enforces system-wide rules structurally, and remains organized around domain meaning rather than utility sprawl.

name: Evolvability and consistency
description: The code can be changed, extended, and deleted safely and cheaply, and it solves problems the way the rest of the codebase already solves them.
details:
This lens looks forward rather than at the present state. Predictable blast radius, support for incremental evolution, deliberate extension points, easy deletion, consistent local conventions, a codebase that is navigable and hard to misuse, a system that is easy to reason about under change, visible long-term cost in local choices, and coherence across the whole product all belong together because they answer one question from different angles: what will the next change cost, and will the next contributor make it correctly.

Strong signs include changes whose likely impact is limited and understandable; improvement available in small safe steps rather than only by rewrite; explicit seams where variation is genuinely likely; code and abstractions that can be removed without triggering hidden dependency mines; similar problems solved with the same naming, structure, and conventions as their neighbours; repository shape and API design that guide contributors to the right place and make incorrect usage conspicuous; obvious answers to where to look and what to protect when requirements change; and local shortcuts either rejected or explicitly acknowledged with their cost. Weak signs include edits whose consequences cannot be bounded, improvements that require touching everything at once, extension by invasive modification of existing paths, dead code no one dares delete, competing local styles for the same problem, structures that make misuse the path of least resistance, behavior that can only be traced by running it, and shortcuts that quietly transfer cost to whoever comes next.

This lens matters because most of a system's cost is paid after it is written, and it is paid by people who were not there when the decisions were made. Consistency and evolvability are what let a codebase absorb years of change without becoming a collection of local micro-cultures. Judge whether the change lowers or raises the cost of the changes that will follow it.
symptoms:
SYM-033 | Blast radius is predictable | The likely impact of changing a rule, dependency, schema, or interface is limited and understandable.
SYM-034 | Incremental evolution is supported | The structure allows change in small safe steps rather than demanding broad rewrites for modest improvements.
SYM-035 | Extension points are deliberate | The system has explicit seams for likely variation instead of forcing invasive modification for every new need.
SYM-036 | Deletion is easy | Dead code, outdated paths, and obsolete abstractions can be removed without fear of hidden dependency mines.
SYM-047 | Local conventions are consistent across the codebase | Similar problems are solved with the same naming, structure, documentation, and cross-cutting conventions so that a reviewer sees one coherent local style instead of competing patterns.
SYM-071 | The codebase is easy to navigate and hard to misuse | Repository shape, API design, and local structure help contributors find the right place to work, guide them toward correct usage, and make incorrect usage conspicuous or difficult.
SYM-072 | The system is easy to reason about under change | When requirements evolve, it is obvious where to look, what to protect, and what else might be affected.
SYM-073 | Long-term cost is visible in local choices | Local shortcuts that create systemic maintenance debt are either rejected or explicitly acknowledged.
SYM-074 | The system behaves like one coherent product | From function semantics up to architecture, the whole system expresses a unified set of rules, patterns, and expectations rather than conflicting local micro-cultures.

name: Operability and production behavior
description: The system can be configured, observed, scaled, migrated, and released by people who did not write it, and its signals reflect what is really happening.
details:
Operability is judged from the position of whoever is on call. Explicit externalized validated configuration, intentional performance and scale behavior, structured and useful logs, diagnostics that preserve signal, health checks that reflect real health, observability aimed at critical paths, survivable data migrations, understood versioning and compatibility, and delivery mechanics that support the intended architecture all belong to one lens because they are answered by the same question: can this be run, watched, and moved forward safely by someone who was not involved in writing it.

Strong signs include environment-dependent behavior configured outside core logic, read in controlled places, and validated early enough to fail before the system runs on broken assumptions; deliberate handling of load and hot paths instead of incidental performance; logs that carry machine-readable context rather than free-form prose; errors, traces, and metrics that make a failure diagnosable without drowning the operator; health and readiness signals that reflect whether the service can actually do its job; instrumentation concentrated on the behaviors users and operators care about; schema and data evolution designed to work across versions and during deployment; explicit handling of evolving contracts, old clients, and deployment skew; and reproducible builds whose quality gates check real risks. Weak signs include configuration read ad hoc deep inside logic or discovered missing at runtime, scale behavior nobody has reasoned about, log lines that cannot be searched or correlated, errors that lose their cause, health checks that return healthy while the dependency is down, blind spots on exactly the paths that matter, migrations that assume a single simultaneous cutover, contract changes that break older clients silently, and pipelines that pass while the real risk goes unchecked.

This lens matters because a system that cannot be operated is unfinished regardless of how good its logic is. Operability defects are discovered during incidents, when the cost of missing information is highest and the people paying it have the least context. Judge whether the change leaves the system easier to run, observe, and evolve in production, or whether it adds behavior that only its author can understand while it is failing.
symptoms:
SYM-030 | Configuration is explicit, externalized, and validated | Environment-dependent behavior is configured outside core logic, read in controlled places, and checked early enough that the system does not run on broken assumptions.
SYM-032 | Performance and scale behavior are intentional | Load handling, hot paths, optimization choices, and scalability are shaped deliberately so the system continues to behave predictably as demand grows without spreading complexity unnecessarily.
SYM-049 | Logs are structured and useful | Production logs carry useful context and machine-readable shape instead of noise or free-form guessing text.
SYM-050 | Diagnostics preserve signal | Errors, traces, and metrics contain enough information to diagnose failures without drowning operators in clutter.
SYM-052 | Health signals reflect real health | Health endpoints and readiness checks reflect whether the service can actually perform its role.
SYM-053 | Observability matches critical paths | The system emits signals around the behaviors that matter most to users and operators.
SYM-068 | Data migrations are survivable | Schema and data evolution are designed to happen safely across versions and deployments.
SYM-069 | Versioning and compatibility are understood | The system handles evolving contracts, clients, data shapes, and deployment skew with intention.
SYM-070 | Delivery mechanics and quality support the intended architecture | Build and delivery behavior is reproducible, quality gates check meaningful risks, and tooling reinforces the architectural shape instead of undermining it.

name: Security privacy and user harm
description: Trust boundaries, privileges, secrets, data exposure, auditability, defaults, and user-facing language protect the people the system touches.
details:
This lens follows trust and consequence. Explicit security boundaries, least privilege, secrets kept out of source, minimized data exposure, auditable sensitive actions, safe defaults, accessibility in user-facing paths, and inclusive language all belong together because they answer one question about the change: who could be harmed by it, and how easily. The harm may be a breach, a privacy violation, an unexplainable action, or a person quietly excluded from using the system, and all of those are decided by the same design choices.

Strong signs include trust levels and privilege transitions that are visible in the code rather than implied; components operating with the minimum permissions they need; credentials and keys supplied from outside the artifact; collection, storage, return, and retention limited to what the purpose requires; telemetry scrubbed of secrets and personal data; security and privacy relevant events traceable after the fact; the easiest path through the code also being the safe one; user-visible output and flows that do not casually exclude people; and naming and messages free of unnecessary exclusionary or misleading language. Weak signs include boundary crossings that are impossible to locate, broad standing permissions granted for convenience, hard-coded tokens or keys, endpoints and logs that return more than the caller needs, sensitive operations that leave no trace, defaults that are insecure or destructive unless someone remembers to change them, interfaces that assume one kind of user, and language that excludes or misleads.

This lens matters because these failures are borne by people who did not choose them and often cannot detect them. They are also among the hardest to remediate after release: exposed data cannot be unexposed, and an embedded secret must be treated as compromised. Judge whether the change reduces the harm the system can do to the people it touches, and whether the safe path is also the easy one.
symptoms:
SYM-051 | Sensitive data is protected in telemetry | Logs, traces, and messages do not leak secrets, private data, or unsafe internal detail.
SYM-054 | Security boundaries are explicit | Trust levels, privilege transitions, and sensitive operations are visible in the design and code paths.
SYM-055 | Least privilege is followed | Code, services, and components operate with the minimum permissions they need.
SYM-056 | Secrets are not embedded | Credentials, tokens, keys, and sensitive configuration are not hard-coded into source or artifacts.
SYM-057 | Data exposure is minimized | The system only collects, stores, returns, and retains what is needed for its legitimate purpose.
SYM-058 | Sensitive actions are auditable | Important security or privacy-relevant events can be traced after the fact.
SYM-059 | Unsafe defaults are avoided | The easiest path through the code does not accidentally produce insecure, destructive, or privacy-harming behavior.
SYM-060 | Accessibility is considered in user-facing paths | User-visible outputs, flows, and interfaces do not casually exclude people through avoidable design choices.
SYM-061 | Inclusive language is used | Naming, docs, messages, and user-facing outputs avoid unnecessary exclusionary or misleading language.

name: Test meaning and evidence
description: The tests state and protect meaningful promises about behavior, cover invariants and unhappy paths, and give a reader enough evidence to trust a pass and diagnose a failure.
details:
This lens reads the tests as specifications. Tests that encode behavior rather than implementation trivia, coverage of important invariants, deliberate exercise of unhappy and edge paths, readable tests, cheap-to-understand setup, restraint with mocking, regression evidence for changed behavior, minimized manual-only verification, evidence behind correctness claims, diagnosable failures, and scope that matches the test's name and intent all belong together because they are answered by the same activity: reading each test and asking what promise it protects and whether a reader could trust it.

Strong signs include test names and assertions that describe externally meaningful behavior; at least one test per important rule that would fail if the rule broke; negative, edge, and misuse cases exercised on purpose; tests a reviewer can read once and understand; setup that makes the preconditions obvious rather than hiding them in fixtures and helpers; assertions on outcomes rather than on every internal interaction; changed behavior backed by a test that proves the intended effect and would catch a relapse; mechanized checks in place of habitual manual verification; correctness claims supported by something executable; failure output that points at the broken behavior; and a name, setup, action, and assertion that all describe the same thing at the same level. Weak signs include tests coupled to internal structure that should be free to change, invariants no test would notice breaking, only-happy-path suites, tests that must be reverse engineered, fixture mazes and magical helpers, mock-interaction assertions standing in for outcomes, behavior changes with no corresponding test, correctness resting on someone having tried it once, failures that require reruns and guesswork, and names that promise more or less than the test checks.

This lens matters because tests are the evidence a reviewer, and every future maintainer, actually relies on. A suite that passes without meaning is worse than no suite: it produces confidence without protection and makes refactoring feel dangerous while proving nothing. Judge whether the change leaves behind trustworthy evidence of the behavior it claims.
symptoms:
SYM-037 | Tests encode behavior, not implementation trivia | Tests describe externally meaningful promises rather than internal structure that should be free to change.
SYM-038 | Important invariants are tested | Each important rule, guarantee, or failure mode has at least one test that would fail if the guarantee broke.
SYM-039 | Happy and unhappy paths are both tested | Negative cases, edge cases, and misuse paths are intentionally exercised rather than left implicit.
SYM-042 | Tests are readable | A reviewer can tell what behavior a test protects and why it matters.
SYM-043 | Test setup is cheap to understand | Creating the conditions for a test does not require navigating a maze of fixtures, mocks, or magical helpers.
SYM-044 | Over-mocking is avoided | Tests do not become brittle by asserting every internal interaction instead of meaningful outcomes.
SYM-045 | Regression evidence exists | Changed behavior is backed by tests or checks that prove the intended effect and protect against relapse.
SYM-046 | Manual-only verification is minimized | Important correctness claims are not left resting on ad hoc human checking when they could be mechanized.
SYM-062 | Evidence backs correctness claims | Assertions that something works are supported by checks, tests, logs, traces, commands, or measurable evidence.
SYM-082 | Test failures are diagnosable | When tests fail, the output gives enough context to understand the broken behavior without guesswork or habitual reruns.
SYM-083 | Test scope matches test name and intent | The name, setup, action, and assertions of a test all describe the same behavior at the same level of abstraction.

name: Test placement and isolation
description: Each test sits at the cheapest layer that can provide trustworthy evidence and is insulated from the world, so results reflect product behavior rather than environment.
details:
This lens judges where tests live and what they depend on. Tests at the right level, unit tests that avoid physical I/O and mock physical boundaries, integration tests that exercise real seams, end-to-end tests reserved for critical journeys, broad shallow release-gating smoke tests, realistically exercised integration points, determinism, owned and isolated test data, and controlled external dependencies all belong to one lens because they are answered by the same reading: for each test, what layer is this, what does it really touch, and does that match the evidence it claims to provide.

Strong signs include behavior verified at the cheapest layer that can be trusted; unit tests that exercise logic without the real filesystem, network, database, or clock unless that resource is the behavior under test; integration tests that cross the real seams where components, adapters, schemas, and configuration meet; a small number of end-to-end tests covering high-value journeys through the deployed shape; smoke tests that quickly answer whether a build or environment is healthy enough to trust; outcomes that do not depend on timing luck, execution order, or leftover state; tests that create and clean up the data they rely on; and third-party systems bounded or replaced so their instability cannot be mistaken for a product defect. Weak signs include logic pushed into slow broad tests because the seams are untestable, unit tests quietly touching the disk, network, or wall clock, integration tests that mock the very boundary they claim to verify, sprawling end-to-end suites used as the primary safety net, smoke tests that have grown into deep assertions, order-dependent or time-sensitive tests, shared mutable fixtures that couple tests to each other, and suites that fail when someone else's service has a bad day.

This lens matters because misplaced tests produce slow, flaky suites that teams learn to ignore, and ignored suites protect nothing. Placement also determines what a failure tells you: a well-levelled failure localizes the defect, while a badly levelled one only reports that something, somewhere, is wrong. Judge whether the change puts its verification where it will stay fast, trustworthy, and informative.
symptoms:
SYM-040 | Integration points are exercised realistically | At least some tests cover real wiring between modules, adapters, and system boundaries.
SYM-041 | Tests are deterministic | Test outcomes do not depend on timing luck, ordering accidents, external state, or flaky infrastructure.
SYM-075 | Tests sit at the right level | Behavior is verified at the cheapest test layer that can provide trustworthy evidence, rather than pushed unnecessarily into broad slow tests.
SYM-076 | Unit tests avoid physical I/O | Unit tests verify focused behavior without touching the real filesystem, network, database, clock, or other physical/environmental resources unless that resource is the behavior under test.
SYM-077 | Integration tests verify real boundaries | Integration tests exercise the real seams where components, adapters, schemas, infrastructure, or configuration meet.
SYM-078 | End-to-end tests protect critical journeys | End-to-end tests cover a small number of high-value user or system journeys through the deployed shape of the application.
SYM-079 | Smoke tests are broad, shallow, and release-gating | Smoke tests quickly determine whether a build, deployment, or environment is healthy enough for deeper testing or use.
SYM-080 | Test data is owned and isolated | Tests create, control, and clean up the data and state they depend on rather than relying on accidental shared conditions.
SYM-081 | External dependencies are controlled in tests | Tests bound or replace nondeterministic third-party systems so failures reflect product behavior rather than outside instability.
SYM-084 | Unit tests mock physical boundaries | Unit tests avoid real filesystem, network, database, clock, process, and environment access unless the physical boundary itself is the behavior under test.
